George IV. King of the United Kingdom from 1820 to 1830, having previously served as Prince Regent during his father George III's mental incapacity. A man of refined cultural taste but volatile temperament and questionable judgment, his reign was marked by political instability, Catholic emancipation struggles, and scandal surrounding his troubled marriage to Caroline of Brunswick.

George IV served as Prince Regent from 1811 to 1820 during his father George III's descent into madness, giving his name to the elegant Regency era of British culture and architecture. The Regency period from 1811 to 1820 saw a flowering of Romantic literature, neoclassical design, and fashionable society centered on the prince's patronage of the arts. He became king at age fifty-seven but faced immediate scandal when he attempted to divorce his estranged queen, Caroline, leading to her public trial on charges of adultery and eventual death in 1821. The Caroline scandal deeply damaged his public reputation, with London crowds supporting Caroline and jeering the king.

He was profoundly influenced by his relationship with Maria Fitzherbert, a Catholic widow whom he married secretly in 1785 before his formal marriage to Caroline. This relationship created constitutional and religious complications for an Anglican monarch. As king, he faced the challenge of Catholic emancipation, which he initially opposed before reluctantly supporting Wellington's Catholic Relief Bill of 1829. He commissioned major construction projects including the renovation of Windsor Castle and development of Regent Street in London, patronizing architecture and the arts. His cultural patronage resulted in some of the finest Regency buildings and interiors in Britain. Yet he was known for lavish spending, heavy drinking, and dissolute personal behavior. He left the throne deeply unpopular, with his final years shadowed by illness and the weight of political conflicts unresolved.
